q6.answer: A fences itself via a lease. A's database host runs a lease agent that renews a 30 s write lease from the external active-region record. The command moves the record to FENCING with active=B, which ends renewals. A partitioned A cannot renew or reach the record, so it sets read-only and stops Postgres when the lease expires. The command waits 35 s (TTL plus 5 s skew margin) before promoting B. A local watchdog covers a hung agent, and a restarted A comes up read-only until the record says active=A.

q7.answer: The active-region record holds it. It is a strongly consistent store with compare-and-set and leases, placed outside both regions. The failover command writes it with CAS (FENCING, B_PROMOTED, B_ACTIVE, plus progress flags) and reads it on every run to find where to resume. A's lease agent reads it and renews against it. Section 1 says nothing about B's side reading it, so I did not decide that.

q8.answer: Rows that were `running` replicate to B still marked `running`. After B is promoted and verified writable, one transaction sets all `running` rows back to `pending`. This happens before B's workers start, so no worker sees a stale `running` row. Jobs are therefore at-least-once, and handlers need idempotency keys. Jobs in the unreplicated WAL tail are lost.

q9.answer: The command is idempotent. Rerunning it reads the record and resumes at the first incomplete step. After B_PROMOTED it only rolls forward and never demotes B. Before promotion succeeds (FENCING, B's database not writable), only a human can deliberately move the record back to active=A with a new epoch, and the command never does this on its own. Once B is promoted, going back to A is not possible, and A would have to be rebuilt as a replica.

q10.answer: The plan does not decide this. DNS moves only after B is healthy, with a 60 s TTL, so a client with a cached record pointing at A should see A's outage until its cache expires. After that it reaches B. I did not specify client behavior beyond the TTL. A is fenced and read-only, so it takes no writes. Users must sign in again on B.

q11.answer: It can lose up to the unreplicated WAL tail, and the real loss is not bounded by the check. The command checks B's last recorded replay lag against 30 s, but that value freezes when A dies, so it understates the loss. A pass means no known violation, not a guarantee. Replication is asynchronous. The command should print the time of the last WAL receipt. The override allows continuing past a lag over 30 s.
